User who had been looking for a good self-hosted UI that supports plugins/functions installed LibreChat, found the install quite easy and said it works very well; plans to replace the UI they were using before.

Critic said LibreChat's main use case seems to be paying under $20/mo for a ChatGPT+-like feature set via APIs, and that it made no real effort to support locally hosted open-source models. They preferred ollama + ollama-webui for a fully local stack (Mistral 7B via docker-compose).

Reply noted LibreChat can connect to local models through a LiteLLM proxy, but the original commenter found it concerning that LibreChat's own LiteLLM docs didn't mention local models as a use case (a GitHub issue was open to add it).

Several users called the name misleading: 'Libre' suggested fully free/local software, but it is mainly an interface to closed chatbots like ChatGPT. One said 'nothing libre about this'; others pointed to gpt4all instead.

User asked what LibreChat offers over kobold.cpp/llama.cpp backends with SillyTavern-style frontends, which already provide local models, TTS voice output, microphone input, Stable Diffusion illustrations and multi-character chats.

User interested because OpenAI trains on ChatGPT chats when history is on, but not on API usage. A self-hosted API client with history appeals to them for use as a diary or note taker. They asked whether LibreChat can import OpenAI history.
'LibreChat was my favorite open source frontend/backend for interacting with LLMs.' After the ClickHouse acquisition, this user finds the overlap tenuous and worries the project will be abandoned.
As a LibreChat user, this commenter is concerned they've seen acquired open source projects soon add paid features and telemetry, and said they might start looking for alternatives.

User who runs LibreChat for personal use called the acquisition 'really bad news' and expects it will eventually be enshittified/monetized. They also felt bad for volunteer contributors who won't benefit.
User has been self-hosting LibreChat for about a year and hoped the developer got a good payout. They questioned how the acquisition helps ClickHouse.

User was concerned about how LibreChat would fund long-term development and saw the acquisition as potentially a good thing. Their biggest worry was that LibreChat might add an SSO tax or enterprise-tier features.

Skeptic called the MIT/open-source promise non-binding and expects eventual license change, citing HashiCorp and Elasticsearch. They argued apps like LibreChat have little technical complexity and many alternatives exist.
